R03-B-01: Most people in the modern West assume that a name is a fixed possession, given once at birth and carried, with perhaps one change at marriage, until death. The assumption is so deep that we rarely notice it is an assumption at all, yet in a wide range of societies a person's name has been expected to change over a lifetime, and one of the commonest occasions for the change is the birth of a child. When a man becomes known as the father of his first child, or a woman as the mother of hers, anthropologists speak of teknonymy: naming a parent through the offspring. The Arabic custom of addressing a man as Abu, 'father of', followed by the name of his eldest son, is perhaps the most familiar instance, but the practice in various forms has been recorded on several continents. It is tempting to read teknonymy as a simple sign that children are prized, and there is something in this. But the more interesting point is what the custom reveals about how such societies understand a person. In a system of fixed names, identity is treated as something an individual owns from the start, and relationships are added to it later, like rooms built onto a house. In a teknonymous system the order is reversed: a person becomes fully visible in social life only by standing in a relationship; the new name announces not that the individual has changed but that their position in a web of kin has changed. One is addressed less as a self than as a point where generations meet. This also explains a feature that puzzles outsiders. In some communities it becomes mildly rude to use the old personal name of an adult who has a child, much as it would be odd for us to call a judge by a childhood nickname in court. The personal name has not been forbidden; it has simply been outranked by a title that carries more social information. Where the practice extends further, so that a grandparent is named after a grandchild, a person's name can track their rise through the generations, and the most senior people come to be known almost entirely through their descendants. None of this should be romanticised, for a system that names people through their children can be hard on those who have none, who may remain, in the language of address, permanently junior. Nor is the Western fixed name as individualistic as it looks, since a surname itself announces a lineage. The contrast is one of emphasis rather than of kind, but the emphasis matters. To change a person's name at the birth of a child is to state, every time that person is greeted, that adulthood is not a private achievement but a place in a sequence.
R03-B-02: National accounts were designed to measure what passes through markets, and for most of their history they have counted the meal bought in a restaurant but not the meal cooked at home, the hour a paid nurse spends with an elderly patient but not the hour a daughter spends with her mother. The omission was never a secret: early statisticians acknowledged it and set it aside as a practical matter, since household work was hard to observe and there was no price at which to record it. The result, however, was a picture of the economy in which a large share of the work that keeps people alive appeared to be no work at all. In recent decades, time-use surveys, in which people record how they spend each part of a day, have made it possible to estimate how many hours households devote to cooking, cleaning and care. Turning those hours into money, however, requires a choice between methods that rest on different assumptions. One method, replacement cost, asks what it would cost to hire someone to do the same tasks. Another, opportunity cost, asks what the person doing the work could have earned in paid employment during those hours. The two methods can produce very different totals, and they can rank the same work differently: an hour of childcare by a surgeon is worth a great deal on the second method and rather little on the first. Critics sometimes take this disagreement as proof that the whole exercise is arbitrary, but that conclusion is too quick. Every figure in national accounts rests on conventions, and the fact that a convention must be chosen does not make zero, the convention long in use, the neutral one. Recording household care at zero is also a valuation, and almost certainly the least accurate available. Estimates, even rough ones, have changed how policy debates can be conducted: they make it harder to describe cuts to public care services as savings when the work has simply moved into homes. There is, nonetheless, a limit to what a price can capture. Both methods treat care as a bundle of tasks that could in principle be handed to someone else. Much of it can be. But part of what a family member provides is the fact that it is they who provide it, and that element has no market equivalent because it cannot be bought. A figure for unpaid care is therefore best understood as a floor rather than a measure: it shows that the work is not nothing, without claiming to say what it is worth.
R03-B-03: When European travellers and administrators first described marriages in which the groom's family transferred cattle, cloth or other goods to the bride's family, many of them reached for the language of the market. The bride, they concluded, was being bought. The description had the appeal of simplicity, and it fitted a ready-made story in which other peoples' customs were cruder versions of the observers' own commercial habits. Words such as 'price' and 'purchase' entered official reports, and they shaped how the custom was seen long after closer study had cast doubt on them. The description also misread, in nearly every important respect, what the transfer did. Consider first where the goods go. In many systems they are not kept by the bride's father as profit but are distributed among a wide circle of her kin, each of whom thereby acquires an interest in the marriage succeeding. Consider next where they go afterwards. Often the cattle received when a daughter marries are the very cattle used to secure a wife for her brother, so that a herd travels from family to family and the transfers form a chain linking households that may never meet. A purchase ends a relationship between buyer and seller; this transfer begins several. Consider, finally, what the transfer secures. In a number of societies what passes with the goods is not the woman herself but the affiliation of her future children to the husband's lineage, which is why, in some of them, the goods must be returned if the marriage ends before any children are born. On this reading, bridewealth is less a price than a contract between groups, and one that gives the bride's family a continuing stake in how she is treated. A family that has shared the goods out among its members, and may have to gather them again in order to return them, has reason both to support the marriage and to intervene when it goes badly. The goods, in other words, work less like a payment than like a pledge, and a pledge held by many hands is harder to ignore than one held by a single man. It would be naive, however, to treat this as the whole story. Where cash has replaced cattle and the sums demanded have risen with the incomes of urban grooms, the transfer can begin to behave much more like a price: it is negotiated against the bride's education or earning power, it is kept by a narrower set of relatives, and young men may delay marriage for years in order to raise it. Critics who see a market in such arrangements are not simply repeating the old error. The lesson is not that the travellers were wrong and the custom is innocent, but that the meaning of a transfer depends on the web of obligations around it, and that when the web thins, the meaning changes.
R03-B-04: Few claims in social history have travelled as far as the idea that childhood was invented. In its best-known form, put forward in the middle of the twentieth century, it held that medieval Europe had no notion of childhood as a distinct stage of life. Children, on this account, passed almost directly from infancy into the company of adults, working, drinking and dressing as they did; painters showed them as miniature men and women; and parents, facing high infant mortality, refrained from investing much feeling in creatures who might not survive. Childhood as we know it, protected, sentimentalised and set apart, was a discovery of the early modern centuries. The thesis was a brilliant provocation, and much of it has not survived. Later historians, reading letters, court records, sermons and the evidence of excavated objects, assembled a large body of material showing that medieval parents grieved for dead children, bought or made toys for living ones, and recognised that the young needed particular kinds of care. The argument from paintings proved especially weak. Artistic conventions are not photographs, and an age that painted saints with golden discs around their heads was not simply reporting what it saw. To infer an absence of feeling from an absence of naturalistic portraiture is to mistake a style for a sentiment. Yet it would be a mistake to conclude that nothing changed. The critics established that medieval people knew children were different and loved them; they did not establish that childhood occupied the same place in social life. What the early modern period did see was the gradual spread of institutions that sorted the young by age and held them apart from adult work: schools divided into classes, a growing literature addressed specifically to children, and eventually laws fixing the ages below which a person could not be employed or married. None of these changes was sudden, and none reached every class or region at once; the children of the poor worked beside adults long after the children of the prosperous had been sent to school. Childhood as a feeling may be ancient. Childhood as a segregated, age-graded stage, organised by institutions, is far more recent. Seen this way, the original thesis and its critics were partly talking past each other. One side asked whether people recognised and cared for children; the other, without always saying so, asked how societies arranged the passage from birth to adult status. This is why the debate could run for so long without resolution: each side could cite evidence the other did not dispute, because each was answering a different question. The second question is the more fruitful, because it leaves room for the observation that every society has children but not every society has childhood in the same form.
R03-B-05: Discussions of population ageing tend to begin with a single number. The old-age dependency ratio divides the number of people above a fixed age, usually sixty-five, by the number of people of working age, conventionally fifteen to sixty-four. As birth rates fall and lives lengthen the ratio rises, and a rising ratio is read as a growing burden: fewer shoulders, it is said, bearing the weight of more pensioners. The image is vivid and the arithmetic is simple, which is precisely why the measure deserves more suspicion than it usually receives. The ratio rests on two equations that are rarely stated. The first is that everyone between fifteen and sixty-four supports others and everyone above sixty-five is supported by them. Neither half is true. Large numbers of people of working age are in education, unemployed, caring full-time for relatives or otherwise outside paid work, while many people beyond the threshold continue to earn, to pay taxes and, perhaps most importantly, to provide unpaid care. In many families it is grandparents whose looking after small children allows both parents to hold jobs; on the ratio's accounting, those grandparents appear only as a cost. The same error runs in the other direction for the many people in their fifties who have left paid work early through illness or redundancy, and who depend on others well before the line is reached. The second equation is that a given age means the same thing in every generation. A sixty-five-year-old today in most countries can expect to live considerably longer, and in better health, than a sixty-five-year-old of the generation in which the threshold was fixed. To keep the line at sixty-five as life expectancy rises is to classify as old an ever larger share of people who are, by the standards that originally justified the line, not old at all. Some demographers have proposed measuring age prospectively, by the years a person can expect still to live rather than the years already lived; on such measures, populations age considerably more slowly than the headline ratio suggests. None of this means that ageing is costless. The final years of a long life often bring a need for intensive medical and personal care, and as more people reach advanced old age that need grows in ways no redefinition can wish away. The objection is not to concern but to calibration. A measure that counts heads by birthday rather than activity by circumstance will tend to exaggerate the problem in its general form and to obscure it in the specific form, very late life, in which it is most acute.
R03-B-06: For much of the twentieth century, anthropologists sorted the ties they recorded into two kinds. Some were 'real', resting on birth and descent; others were 'fictive', a convenient label for godparents, sworn brothers, adopted children and the many other relations that people treated as kinship but that did not, so the observer thought, rest on blood. The distinction seemed merely descriptive, and it took some time to see that it carried a theory with it: that the true foundation of kinship is biological, and that everything else is imitation. The difficulty is that many of the people being described did not share the theory. In a number of societies, people become kin by eating food grown on the same land, by living in the same house, or by being nursed at the same breast. Under Islamic law, for instance, children nursed by the same woman are barred from marrying one another, much as siblings by birth would be; the tie created by milk is not a metaphor for kinship but a form of it. In such places, ties made in these ways may carry the same obligations of help, hospitality and mourning as ties of birth. Where relatedness is understood to accumulate through feeding and sharing over years, to call such ties fictive is not to describe them but to overrule the people who live them. This is not an argument that biology is irrelevant. Birth is, almost everywhere, one of the most powerful ways of reckoning who belongs to whom, and an attempt to dissolve it entirely into choice would be its own kind of distortion. The point is narrower: biology is one idiom of relatedness among several, and which idioms count, and how much, varies from place to place. Nor is the West an exception that proves the biological rule. Adoption, the blended families formed by remarriage, and the arrangements made possible by donated eggs and sperm all require people to decide, often painfully, whether a tie of birth or a tie of care should prevail when the two come apart. Seen this way, kinship is something people do as well as something they are born into. The older vocabulary was not useless, since it pointed to real differences in the ways ties are formed and maintained. Its error lay in treating one culture's answer to the question of what makes people kin as the standard against which every other answer was to be measured, and in mistaking that answer for a fact of nature rather than a choice that other peoples had made differently.
R03-B-07: Every few years a new generation is given a name, and with the name comes a character. One cohort is said to be idealistic and later complacent, another cynical, another anxious, entitled or unusually attached to its telephones. The labels are used by marketers, journalists and employers with a confidence that would be remarkable in any other classification of human beings. We would hesitate to say that everyone born under a given star sign shares a temperament; we say something not very different, and with far less hesitation, about everyone born within a given span of fifteen years. The labels are also remarkably durable: once a cohort has been named and described, the description tends to follow it into middle age, revised only when a newer cohort arrives to take its place as the subject of worry. The trouble begins with a problem of method that social scientists have long recognised. When one group of people differs from another, the difference may reflect their age (the young almost everywhere change jobs more often than the middle-aged), the period in which they are observed (everyone, of whatever age, was affected by a recession or a new technology), or the cohort into which they were born, meaning a lasting imprint left by the conditions of their early years. Only the last is a generational effect in the strict sense. But the three are bound together by arithmetic: a person's age is simply the current year minus the year of birth, so that once any two are known the third is fixed. No set of observations can by itself pull them apart; some assumption from outside the data is always required. Much of what is confidently attributed to a generation turns out, on inspection, to be what people of that age have always done, or what people of every age were doing at the time. A second difficulty concerns boundaries. The years at which one generation is said to end and the next to begin are chosen by convention, and different sources disagree about them by several years. A person born on the last day of one span and a person born on the first day of the next are assigned different characters, while two people born fourteen years apart within one span are assigned the same. Differences within a labelled cohort, by class, region, education and much else, are typically far larger than the differences between cohorts, which is to say that the label groups people along the axis on which they least differ. None of this shows that generations are a fiction. There is a serious idea buried under the marketing: that people who come of age during a war, a depression or a political upheaval may carry its mark for life, and may differ in lasting ways from those who met the same events earlier or later in their lives. Such effects have been found, and they are not trivial. But they are anchored to events rather than to calendars; they mark some members of a cohort far more deeply than others, depending on where and how the event touched them; and they rarely produce a single character that an entire cohort shares. Why, then, do the calendar labels persist? Part of the answer is that they are convenient, turning a tangle of causes into a story with protagonists. Part of it is that they flatter, inviting each cohort to see itself as distinctive and its elders or juniors as the problem. The cost of the story is easy to miss. When young adults find housing unaffordable or work insecure, attributing their situation to a generational temperament converts a question about economic arrangements into a question about character, and a question about character has no obvious policy answer.
R03-B-08: There is a familiar story about the family in South Asia. Once, it runs, people lived in large joint households: an elderly couple, their married sons with wives and children, perhaps unmarried daughters and a widowed aunt, all sharing one roof, one kitchen and one purse under the authority of the eldest man. Then came cities, salaried jobs and the ideal of the companionate couple, and the joint family began to break up into small units of parents and children. The story is told with pride by those who see the old household as a school of duty and with relief by those who see it as a school of obedience, but both versions agree about the direction of travel. It is repeated by planners, preachers and novelists alike, and it is so familiar that it is rarely asked for its evidence. The evidence for the story is weaker than its popularity suggests. Much of it comes from counting households at a single moment, and a single moment is a poor guide to a process that unfolds over decades. A joint household is not a permanent structure but a phase. A young couple may live alone for some years; the household becomes joint when a son marries and brings his wife home; it may grow when a second son does the same; and it often divides when the father dies and the brothers set up separate hearths, each of which may in turn become joint a generation later. In a population in which every family followed this cycle exactly, a count taken on any given day would find a great many nuclear households, even though nearly everyone would spend part of life in a joint one. A high proportion of nuclear households, then, is not by itself evidence that the joint family is disappearing. The wider theory behind the story fares little better. It was long assumed that industry produced the nuclear family, by moving work out of the home and rewarding people who could move to wherever the jobs were. Yet historians of north-western Europe found that small households of parents and children were already common there long before the factories arrived; if anything, the causation may have run partly the other way. A society's household form, it seems, is not simply read off its economy. This is not to say that nothing has changed. Migration for work has scattered many families across cities and countries, so that brothers who would once have shared a courtyard now live hundreds of kilometres apart. But dispersal is not the same thing as dissolution. Money flows back to parents; decisions about marriages, property and the education of children are still taken together; a son abroad may be more bound by his family's expectations than a son next door. Some families keep a common fund into which brothers in different cities pay, and from which the costs of weddings and illnesses are met. A census that defines the joint family by shared residence will record such a family as several nuclear ones, and will miss the jointness that matters most to its members. It would be equally mistaken to swing to the opposite view and declare the joint family unchanged. What is being renegotiated, often bitterly, is less the size of the household than the authority within it: whether a daughter-in-law must defer to her mother-in-law, whether elders decide whom the young marry, whether property passes to sons alone. The quarrels are often sharpest where the household is still shared, because shared space turns every question of precedence into a daily one. These are real changes, and they are better described as a transformation of jointness than as its end.
